title: Jury rules on man's death; Excited delirium cited as cause Training on risks urged for police: [ONT Edition]
article: A coroner's jury has ruled that excited delirium and restraint asphyxia caused the accidental death of Nicholas Blentzas, a 24- year-old man who died in police custody nearly three years ago.

After hearing 21 witnesses, the five-person jury also recommended that police officers, police recruits and court officers receive enhanced and continued training in the signs and symptoms of excited delirium and its risks.
It also asked that officers, recruits and court workers be trained in the risks associated with the physical restraint of those experiencing an episode of excited delirium.

Evidence was given during the inquest that Blentzas had suffered from excited delirium, a medical condition that can occur in psychiatric patients who have gone off their medication. It can also occur in alcoholics and cocaine addicts.

The condition is considered a medical emergency, increases blood pressure, heart and respiratory rates, and can cause cardiac arrhythmia, testified Jim Cairns, Ontario's deputy chief coroner. Anyone suffering from it needs immediate hospitalization.

Blentzas, who suffered from an ongoing and degenerating mental illness, died in the early hours of June 23, 2002, after a struggle with police. Neighbours had called police because Blentzas was trying to break into his own apartment with a fire extinguisher. Police found him there, sweating and shirtless and acting strangely.

They managed to talk him into going with them to the hospital, but at the last minute he bolted. Officers tried to subdue him with pepper spray, but it didn't work. Eventually, they wrestled him to the ground and handcuffed him. He died before paramedics arrived. The Special Investigations Unit cleared the police of any wrongdoing.

Nicholas Blentzas' brother Jim was subdued as he listened to the jury's decision but felt something good came out of the tragedy. "What's positive is the jury recognized that it was more than natural causes," he said.

"It was related to the way the police attempted to make their apprehension.... This went beyond unavoidable circumstances and hopefully in the future it will be avoidable. I'm glad that they added they will now provide training for new recruits or any police officers that excited delirium is in fact a medical emergency."

The jury also heard testimony that certain restraint positions, including being held in a prone position with hands behind the back, can cause restraint asphyxia and death. Some witnesses at the trial testified that they saw Blentzas held down with his arms behind his back.

"It's clear that the jury felt that education with respect to excited delirium is of fundamental importance," said David Carruthers, counsel for the coroner's office. "And if enhanced or continued training of police officers about this issue helps save lives then everyone would agree that's a good thing."
